596.title: Head on the arm
596.hook: a quiet prayer of confession, head resting on the arm, left out on happy days
596.howItsDone: On ordinary weekdays, after the morning and afternoon Amidah, many Jews say Tachanun, in many Ashkenazi communities resting the head on the forearm; it is omitted on Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh, Hanukkah, Purim, all of Nisan, Tisha b'Av and in other joyful circumstances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last words of the Amidah: my God, guard my tongue. Your line was guard my tongue. Did your guarded hour hold? Today, the Amidah is over, and the service goes somewhere lower. Day five hundred ninety-six.

Walk into a weekday morning service right after the Amidah and you might see something that looks like a room full of tired students. People sit down, lean forward, and rest their foreheads on their forearms, like a kid with their head down on the desk. The room goes quiet. Nobody's asleep. They're saying a prayer that's meant to be said from that low place. And on some days, the happiest ones, the whole thing is simply skipped.
screen: `HEADS DOWN, LIKE STUDENTS AT DESKS.` → `NOBODY'S ASLEEP.` → `SKIPPED ON HAPPY DAYS.`

segments.voice: It's called Tachanun, supplication, pleading. Its oldest form is nefilat apayim, falling on the face. In the Bible, Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before God; so does Joshua, after a defeat. In the time of the Talmud, people seem to have stretched out on the ground. Today, in many Ashkenazi communities, it's become the head resting on the arm. Many Sephardi communities say it sitting, without lowering the head. The words are honest and low. One line, from King David, is said in many communities just before: in the old Jewish translation, "let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for His mercies are great; and let me not fall into the hand of man." David has done wrong and is given a choice of punishments. He chooses to be in God's hands rather than in human hands, because God's mercy is bigger. Then, in the Ashkenazi rite, Psalm 6: I am weary with my groaning. And here's the surprising part. Tachanun is left out on days that are joyful. Shabbat and festivals. The new month. Hanukkah and Purim. The whole month of Nisan. When there's a groom in the room in the week after his wedding, or a father whose baby is having his bris that day. Even, strangely, on Tisha b'Av, because the prophet calls it, in a sense, a festival, a day of future comfort. The tradition knows there's a time to put your head down, and a time not to.
screen: `TACHANUN: PLEADING.` · `FROM FALLING ON THE FACE TO THE ARM.` · `INTO GOD'S HANDS, NOT HUMAN HANDS.` · `LEFT OUT ON JOYFUL DAYS.` · then, large: `LOW AND HONEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your head and be honest. If you're sitting at a table or desk, lean forward and rest your forehead on your forearm. If not, just lower your head. Let your shoulders drop. From down here, say one honest thing: where you fell short this week, or what you're tired of carrying. Don't argue with it, don't fix it. Just let it be said, low. If you pray, you can say it into God's hands. When you're ready, sit up slowly. The bell holds the time.
Tachanun. Supplication. The prayer after the Amidah, said with the head down on the arm, and left out on joyful days.
Your line: low and honest. Today, let one person hear an honest sentence from you about something hard, said plainly, without dressing it up. Day five hundred ninety-six.

597.title: The ark opens
597.hook: the congregation stands as the Torah is carried around and greeted with a kiss
597.howItsDone: On Monday and Thursday mornings, Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh and fast days, the ark is opened and the congregation stands; the Torah is carried around the synagogue, and people touch its cover with a tallit fringe or prayer book and kiss it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tachanun, the head on the arm. Your line was low and honest. Did someone hear one plain, honest sentence from you? Today, the room stands up again, and the doors at the front swing open. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

On Monday and Thursday mornings, on Shabbat, festivals and the new month, the service reaches a moment that feels like a parade in a very small space. Someone pulls back a curtain at the front of the room. The doors behind it open. Everyone stands. A scroll in a velvet cover, or a carved wooden case, is lifted out and carried through the aisles. People reach out as it passes. A woman touches it with the corner of her prayer book. A child is lifted up to kiss it.
screen: `A CURTAIN PULLED BACK.` → `EVERYONE STANDS.` → `A PARADE IN A SMALL SPACE.`

segments.voice: Why those days? The Talmud, in Bava Kamma 82a, says the prophets made sure the people never went three days without Torah, and Ezra the scribe set readings for Mondays and Thursdays, market days, when people came into town. So the Torah is read on those mornings, on Shabbat, and on special days. As the ark opens, many congregations sing a verse Moses said when the ark set out in the wilderness. In the old Jewish translation: "Rise up, O LORD, and let Thine enemies be scattered." Then a line from Isaiah: "for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem." The ark in the synagogue is named for that traveling ark; Ashkenazim call it the aron kodesh, the holy ark, and Sephardim often call it the heichal, the palace. Everyone stands while it's open. The Talmud, in Kiddushin, argues: if people rise for those who study the Torah, how much more for the Torah itself. Then the scroll is carried around. People don't usually touch the parchment; they touch the cover with the fringes of their tallit or the edge of a prayer book, and kiss that. In many Sephardi communities, the scroll lives in a hard case and stands upright to be read. Notice what's happening. The most precious object in the room isn't locked away or kept on a stage. It's brought down the aisles, close enough to touch, and everyone gets to greet it.
screen: `NEVER THREE DAYS WITHOUT TORAH.` · `RISE UP, O LORD.` · `STAND FOR THE TORAH ITSELF.` · `CARRIED DOWN THE AISLES.` · then, large: `STAND FOR THE SCROLL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand for something precious. Think of one thing in your home that carries more than its weight: a grandparent's book, a photo, a letter, a ring, a child's first drawing. If you can, go and stand in front of it, or stand where you are and picture it clearly. Stand still for a moment, the way you'd stand for someone who walked into the room. Notice what it carries for you. If you like, touch it gently, the way people touch the scroll. The bell holds the time.
The ark opens. The moment the Torah is taken out, the congregation stands, and the scroll is carried through the room and kissed.
Your line: stand for the scroll. Today, when someone you respect walks into the room, stand up, or at least stop what you're doing and greet them properly. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

598.title: The pointer
598.hook: the reader follows the words with a silver hand, so the scroll isn't touched
598.howItsDone: During the Torah reading, the reader follows the text with a yad, a pointer ending in a small hand, while gabbaim follow in a printed chumash and correct errors; those called up touch the scroll with a tallit fringe or its cover and kiss it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ark opened and the room stood. Your line was stand for the scroll. Did you greet someone properly when they came in? Today, the scroll is open on the table, and a small silver hand appears. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

Imagine reading aloud, in front of a hundred people, from a page with no punctuation, no vowels, no paragraph numbers, and no notes on how to sing it. Just columns of black Hebrew letters, written by hand, on parchment, in a text you must not get wrong by a single word. And you can't put your finger on the line to keep your place. That's the job of the Torah reader every week. And there's a small tool on the table to help, shaped like a hand.
screen: `NO VOWELS, NO PUNCTUATION.` → `NOT A SINGLE WORD WRONG.` → `A TOOL SHAPED LIKE A HAND.`

segments.voice: It's called a yad: Hebrew for hand. A slim rod, often silver, sometimes wood, ending in a tiny hand with one finger pointing. The reader holds it just above the parchment and moves it word by word. Why not just use a finger? Two reasons. First, the scroll itself is fragile and holy. Every letter is written by a trained scribe, a sofer, with a quill and special ink, and a smudged or broken letter can make the whole scroll unfit until it's repaired. Hands carry oil and sweat. Second, there's a teaching in the Talmud, in Megillah 32a, that holding a Torah scroll with bare hands is a kind of disrespect. So people touch it with something else: the fringe of a tallit, the cover, or the yad. The yad itself is a custom, not a law spelled out in the Talmud, but it has spread so widely that it's hard to picture a reading without one. Because the scroll has no vowels or musical notes, the reader has prepared for hours, sometimes days. Two people stand on either side, following in a printed book with all the vowels and notes, ready to quietly correct a mistake. And the person called up to bless the reading touches the place with their tallit fringe and kisses it. Notice what the yad teaches without a word. The point isn't the hand. It's what the hand points to. A good teacher, a good parent, a good friend works the same way.
screen: `YAD: A HAND THAT POINTS.` · `A SMUDGED LETTER, AN UNFIT SCROLL.` · `NO VOWELS, NO NOTES: PREPARED BY HEART.` · `THE POINT IS WHAT IT POINTS TO.` · then, large: `A HAND THAT POINTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow a text with your finger. Pick up something written: a book, a letter, a page of scripture, even a recipe. Choose a few lines. Read them slowly, moving your finger, or a pen, just under each word as you go. Don't let your eyes run ahead of your hand. Notice how much slower it is, and how much more you see: small words, odd spellings, a phrase you'd usually skim. If it's a sacred text for you, let the pointing be a kind of respect. The bell holds the time.
Yad. Hand. The pointer the Torah reader uses to follow the words without touching the parchment.
Your line: a hand that points. Today, when you help someone, point them toward the answer instead of handing it over. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

599.title: Lifting the scroll
599.hook: the open scroll is raised high for everyone to see
599.howItsDone: At hagbah, one person lifts the open Torah scroll and turns to show the congregation, who sing V'zot haTorah; in most Ashkenazi communities this follows the reading and in most Sephardi communities it precedes it, and a second person, the golel, rolls and dresses the scroll.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yad, the silver hand. Your line was a hand that points. Did you point someone toward an answer instead of handing it over? Today, the scroll leaves the table and goes up. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

A person walks up to the reading table and takes hold of the two wooden rollers of an open Torah scroll. The scroll is heavy, and it's open several columns wide. They slide it to the edge of the table, bend their knees, and in one motion lift it high over their head, arms spread, the columns of letters facing the room. Then they turn slowly, so everyone can see. Some people stretch out a finger toward it. Some sing. Nobody breathes much until it's safely down.
screen: `TWO WOODEN ROLLERS.` → `LIFTED HIGH, ARMS SPREAD.` → `TURNING SO EVERYONE CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: It's called hagbah, lifting. The person who does it lifts the scroll open, often wide enough that at least three columns show, and turns so that every part of the room can see the writing. A later rabbinic handbook for scribes, tractate Soferim, describes the scroll being shown to everyone, men and women, so all could see the letters and bow. As it's raised, the congregation sings: this is the Torah that Moses set before the children of Israel. The first half comes from Deuteronomy. In the old Jewish translation: "And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel." There's an echo of a much older scene. When Ezra the scribe gathered the people in Jerusalem to read the Torah, the book of Nehemiah says that he opened the book in the sight of all the people, "and when he opened it, all the people stood up." The timing differs. In most Ashkenazi communities, the lifting comes after the reading. In most Sephardi communities, it comes before. Then a second person, the golel, rolls the scroll closed and dresses it again in its cover. The Talmud, in Megillah 32a, gives that rolling a surprising honor: the one who rolls the scroll receives the reward of all the readers. Notice what hagbah does. The text isn't just read to people. It's shown. Lifted out of the hands of experts and turned toward everyone, so the whole room can see it's real.
screen: `HAGBAH: LIFTING.` · `THIS IS THE TORAH MOSES SET BEFORE US.` · `EZRA OPENED IT; ALL STOOD.` · `ASHKENAZI AFTER, SEPHARDI BEFORE.` · then, large: `LIFT IT UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift something up to share it. Think of something you love that other people rarely get to see: a book that changed you, a grandmother's recipe, a photo, a song, a skill you're quietly good at. Picture showing it to someone today. Not explaining it to death. Just holding it up, so they can see it for themselves. Who would you show it to? Settle on one person and one thing. Breathe, and let yourself look forward to it. The bell holds the time.
Hagbah. Lifting. The open Torah scroll raised high and turned so everyone in the room can see the writing.
Your line: lift it up. Today, show the person you pictured the thing you chose, and let them see it for themselves. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

600.title: The prophets answer
600.hook: a reading from the prophets follows the Torah on Shabbat and festivals
600.howItsDone: On Shabbat, festivals and fast days the maftir reads the closing verses of the Torah portion and then chants the haftarah from the Prophets, with blessings before and after; many bar and bat mitzvah students chant it as their portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hagbah, the scroll lifted for everyone to see. Your line was lift it up. Did you show someone the thing you love? Today, after the Torah is rolled closed, a second reading begins. Day six hundred.

Ask someone who had a bar or bat mitzvah what they chanted, and many will say: my haftarah. They'll remember the months of practice, the strange melody, the moment their voice cracked in front of the whole family. Some can still sing a few lines decades later. But ask what a haftarah actually is, and why it comes after the Torah, and the answer often gets fuzzy. It's one of the most familiar parts of the service, and one of the least explained.
screen: `MY HAFTARAH.` → `THE VOICE THAT CRACKED.` → `FAMILIAR, AND RARELY EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: On Shabbat, festivals and fast days, after the Torah reading, one more person is called up, the maftir. They read the last few verses of the Torah portion again, and then a passage from the Prophets: from books like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Samuel or Kings. That passage is the haftarah. The word comes from a root that means to conclude, to complete. It isn't a half of anything; it's the closing reading. Each haftarah is chosen to answer the Torah portion. When the Torah tells of Moses sending spies into the land, the haftarah tells of Joshua sending spies to Jericho. Around the summer fast of Tisha b'Av, the pattern takes over the calendar: three haftarot of warning before the fast, then seven of comfort after it. The first of those seven opens Isaiah forty. In the old Jewish translation: "Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God." So a whole season of the year is shaped by the prophets. Why read the Prophets at all? A popular explanation, written down in the Middle Ages, says that when a foreign king banned Torah reading, Jews read matching passages from the Prophets instead. Historians aren't sure that's how it began; the Mishnah already treats the reading as long established. Either way, the structure says something. The Torah speaks, and the prophets answer: later voices taking up the same story, centuries on, and asking what it means now.
screen: `THE MAFTIR READS THE PROPHETS.` · `HAFTARAH: THE CONCLUDING READING.` · `CHOSEN TO ANSWER THE PORTION.` · `COMFORT YE, MY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `THE PROPHETS ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of a prophet. If you have a Bible nearby, open to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos or Micah, anywhere, and read one line slowly. If you don't, take the line from today: comfort ye, comfort ye My people. Say it once, quietly. Then ask: who might have needed to hear this, the day it was first said? And who might need to hear it today? Let one face come to mind. The bell holds the time.
Haftarah. The concluding reading. A passage from the Prophets read after the Torah, chosen to answer it.
Your line: the prophets answer. Today, when you hear an old story or old advice, ask what a later voice would say back to it. Day six hundred.

601.title: Prayers for others
601.hook: blessings for the sick, the community and the country
601.howItsDone: During the Torah service, Mi Sheberach blessings are said for those called up, for the sick, whose names are added aloud or whispered to the leader, and for the congregation; many synagogues also say prayers for the country and for the State of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the haftarah, the reading from the Prophets. Your line was the prophets answer. Did a later voice answer an old story for you? Today, the prayers said around the open scroll, for other people. Day six hundred one.

While the Torah lies open on the table, there's a pause between readings. Someone walks up to the person leading and whispers a name. Then another. Then a list on a scrap of paper. A neighbor's husband after surgery. A cousin's newborn. A friend in rehab. The leader starts a short prayer, and when it reaches the gap, the names pour in, sometimes for a full minute. In some congregations, people simply stand and say them out loud, one after another, until the room goes quiet again.
screen: `A NAME WHISPERED TO THE LEADER.` → `A LIST ON A SCRAP OF PAPER.` → `THE NAMES POUR IN.`

segments.voice: The prayer begins Mi sheberach avoteinu: may the One who blessed our ancestors, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in many communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, bless this person. It's a formula, a frame, and almost anything can go in it. There's a Mi Sheberach for each person called up to the Torah. A Mi Sheberach for the sick, asking for complete healing of body and spirit, where you'll hear the names from that scrap of paper. One for the whole congregation, and for everyone who gives to it and serves it. One for a new baby, one for a couple about to marry. Many synagogues also say a prayer for the country and its leaders, and in many communities one for the State of Israel and those who defend it. Praying for the government has deep roots. When the prophet Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, he tells them, in the old Jewish translation: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Not your city. Their city. And in Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests, says to pray for the welfare of the government, because without it, people would swallow one another alive. In recent decades a sung version of the prayer for healing, by the songwriter Debbie Friedman, has become loved in many synagogues. The frame stays the same: the blessing that reached our ancestors, asked for someone else.
screen: `MAY THE ONE WHO BLESSED OUR ANCESTORS.` · `FOR THE SICK, THE CALLED UP, THE NEW.` · `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · `PRAY FOR THE GOVERNMENT'S WELFARE.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your town. Settle, and breathe. Picture the place you live: the main street, the school, the hospital, the bus stop, the people you pass without knowing their names. Picture the people who run it, the ones you voted for and the ones you didn't. Hold one wish for the whole place: safety, fairness, enough. If you pray, you can ask for its peace. If not, just let yourself care, for a minute, about people you'll never meet. The bell holds the time.
Mi Sheberach. May the One who blessed. The prayer said around the Torah for the sick, the congregation, and the country.
Your line: pray for the city. Today, do one small thing for your town: pick up litter, thank a bus driver, read one local news story all the way through. Day six hundred one.

602.title: Our duty to praise
602.hook: once a High Holy Day prayer, now said at the end of every service
602.howItsDone: Aleinu is said standing at the end of the morning, afternoon and evening services, and many people bend the knees and bow at the line about bending the knee; on the High Holy Days many congregations kneel and prostrate fully during it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mi Sheberach: the blessing for the sick, the community and the country. Your line was pray for the city. Whose name did you hold up? Today, the prayer that closes almost every service. Day six hundred two.

Walk into almost any synagogue near the end of a service, morning, afternoon or evening, and you'll hear the same thing. People stand. The tune picks up. And at one line, the whole room bends its knees and bows, together. It feels like it has always been the ending. It hasn't. For a long stretch of Jewish history, this prayer was heard mainly on Rosh Hashanah, in the most solemn part of the year. Then, sometime in the Middle Ages, it moved. Out of the High Holy Days, and into every single day.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM BOWS.` → `ONCE A NEW YEAR PRAYER.` → `NOW EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Its first word is aleinu: it is upon us. It is our duty. The opening says, roughly, it is our duty to praise the Master of all, to give greatness to the one who formed the world. Then comes the bowing line: and we bend the knee and bow and give thanks before the King of kings. That's when people bow. Where did it come from? Tradition credits Joshua. Many scholars connect it with the third-century sage Rav in Babylonia, who arranged the Rosh Hashanah prayers about God's kingship, and Aleinu opens that section. On the High Holy Days it still keeps its old drama: in many synagogues the cantor, and sometimes everyone, kneels and lowers all the way to the floor. It's one of the only times in the Jewish year that happens. The second paragraph turns outward, toward a hope. It looks to a day when the world will be repaired under the kingship of God. The Hebrew phrase there, l'taken olam, to repair the world, is one of the roots of the modern words tikkun olam. And it ends with a verse from Zechariah, in the old Jewish translation: "And the LORD shall be King over all the earth; in that day shall the LORD be One, and His name one." So the prayer moves in two steps. First, our duty to praise, right now, on our knees. Then the hope that one day the whole world will join in. You walk out of the service with both in your pocket.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow at we bend the knee. Stand, if you can, and settle your breath. If you pray, you can say the opening line in your own language: it is our duty to praise. When you reach we bend the knee and bow, do just that. Bend your knees a little. Bow from the waist. Come back up slowly. Then stay standing and breathe, and let your body remember what it just said. The bell holds the time.
Aleinu. It is upon us. The prayer of duty and hope that closes the service, with a bow in the middle.

Your line: our duty to praise. A week of Tachanun, the ark opening, the yad, lifting the scroll, the haftarah, Mi Sheberach and Aleinu. Today, praise one thing out loud that you'd usually pass by. Day six hundred two.
